blocks.html: After joining Cure.fit as an intern in 2018, I realized the importance of a portfolio that reflects not just my work, but also my approach and personality. With recruiters inundated with portfolio links, I aimed to design a captivating and concise portfolio to make the most of their limited time.

There are multiple ways in which one can share a portfolio, and it can be a portfolio pdf, Behance, or Dribbble link, website etc. Where most of the online portfolios like Dribbble help designers share what they are up to, mainly focussing on visuals and UI. These platforms are perfect for reach and online presence, but most of the time, companies are not looking for such content.
In my case, I decided to have a website as my portfolio for the following reasons:

items: Centralized Content: - Having all my content in one place makes it easier for recruiters to navigate and view my work without the need to open multiple links.
Adding Personality - A website allows me to present my work in a way that tells a cohesive story and reflects my personality, making a stronger impression on potential employers..
Overcoming PDF Limitations - PDF portfolios can be cumbersome to download, which may deter users from viewing them. A website eliminates these issues, providing a seamless browsing experience.
SEO (Benefits) By optimizing my website for search engines, I can attract organic traffic and increase the visibility of my portfolio to a wider audience.

blocks.html: I was just starting my career back then and I was good that I did my research to understand the market before jumping to explorations. Articles online really helped me know for whom to design and what to design. I studied several articles on medium, smashing design, nngroup, and other sources about designing portfolios. Checking other portfolios on the web was also a crucial part of the exploration, how they are trying to solve problems and trying to find out the reasons behind some decisions.
Being on my internship, I also talked to a few designers over there to understand what they look for in a portfolio.

Making sure that users can easily navigate through your content is an essential aspect for every product. Once I was evident with the users' intent and what are the things to be focused, it wasn’t tough to work on navigation.

The idea was to make it simple and sweet, content being the hero and serving the purpose rightfully. I decided to follow a minimal approach for my portfolio and focus on creating the right story with a high focus on the case studies.

It was challenging to get sure of the visuals, it should not only give a unique personality to it but also empower the content. It took me some time and quite some iterations, but in the end, the result was satisfactory.

Every page has its story and for this page the story was about my life. I wanted to make sure anyone who lands on this page gets to know my professional as well as the personal self, Who is Kunal Satpal? What he believes in? What does he enjoy?, and what matters to him the most? Everything had to be answered.

I was no developer back then, it took me quite some time to perfect every part of it, but in the end, it was amazing, and I also learned a lot about development in the process. Thanks a lot to Praduman Goyal and Dhruv Bhanushali for helping me out with this.

Three lines of code to every page and this powerful tool allowed me to analyze user behavior, track drop rates, bounce rates, exits, and session time etc. With Google Analytics, I can gain insights into different cohorts and time frames, helping me understand and optimize my website's performance.

The launch is where the real journey started; I got several messages on social media from people who liked the website and also who found bugs. I also got a handful of feedback on my website, from the readability, layout to the content.
Launching was just the first step, the following section is the journey of how and why I kept on experimenting with my portfolio and what all I learned in this time.
What to do once it is is launched?

items: By putting out your portfolio on the web and showcasing people. You’ll get lots of love and feedback at the same time.
Keep it alive, present it to as many people and designers possible, know their views/feedback for the same.
Don’t hesitate with the feedback and note them all.

blocks.html: One significant feedback I got from my colleague Sai Nihas- “There is much description on the home page, what purpose does it serve”

Considering our target users are busy individuals who are often overwhelmed with numerous websites. Having excessive text and content on the home page could lead to cognitive overload and a high risk of quick drop outs. Given their low attention span, our users needed something easily consumable to capture their interest within a few seconds.

With the help of google analytics I found that the average session duration increased tremendously and drops from home page also reduced. It was so good that I checked them thrice before jumping to conclusions.
This website is still evolving, and with hotjar integration, the heat maps, misclicks, scroll percentage, etc. I was able to know more about the user behaviour.
In february 19 when I was looking for internships, a sudden roadblock occured, my last two projects both were under NDA and I can not share them publicly i.e. I can’t put them on my website.
This is when I decided to create a pass key system that will let users view the case study on the website itself if they have the pass key.
Hotjar provided the data for the deep scroll, the miss clicks and screen recordings.
With the increasing number of articles, case studies, blogs it was really tough to keep the scroll limited. Even adding one case study to the website means adding a full page, this wasn’t scalable.

small With a small stack of cards, more content can be fitted in the same screen size, description and subheading had to be removed to avoid cognitive overload. It also helped in differentiating between case studies and blogs moreover emphasizing on the bigger cards of case studies.

With more than a year passed, a number of things changed in my website several articles were added and now things had to be curated and images to be reduced so that website speed is not compromized. At the same time due to the lack of guidelines for imagery there was inconsistency in various cover images used across the website.
Final covers look like this.
Designing imagery for a blue based website is not that difficult but when everyone started associating this with my identity it hit me hard. A number of people ask me if I’m a big fan of blue?
People got really confused with the home page asking for a passkey, without providing any context. The next page seems very unexpected.
The card still feels not big enough to some users for proper visibility of the content.
Removed color from my brand and identity to avoid biasis and also using black to show professionalism and expertise in my work.
With the imput field upfront and the subheading it is much more clear now what is the meaning of passkey and what exactly is a protected case study.
Using clear and visible images, interaction gifs to give an enhanced visual experience to the user at the same time engaging them with the content. Also opening space for a lot more creative ideas
So far I've got a good reposnse from people on the changes, It'll still takes a few weeks to get the proper data and analyse if these changes worked or not.

Update 2021: Launched in 2020 I saw a great increase in the CTR's and engagement on my website. Moreover it opened to a new place for me add in more engagig content further helping me drive users forward. This portfolio also helped me get into interviews while looking out in 2022 and finally join Gojek.

It had been quite some time since I last reviewed my portfolio. Amidst my busy schedule, I had not had the opportunity to revisit its core elements. However, when I finally took the time to assess it, I recognized some significant gaps, with the primary one being the lack of personality. While the monochrome branding had its advantages, it fell short in terms of character and individuality.

I looked at a bunch of other portfolios and started experimenting with particles, characters, illustrations, and some ideas like merging engineering with design. Another concept transformed the initial wireframe into a full website as users scrolled. Sounds great right? But I wanted more—I wanted my portfolio to reflect my personality.

One day, as I was reorganizing my desk to make it more productive, it suddenly struck me. I realized that my desk contained everything I needed and also represented the kind of person I am. It was filled with games, books, notepads, pens, and coffee mug, all of which perfectly captured my interests and what brings me joy

During my exploration, I experimented with several variations of this idea. One concept involved showcasing a top view of a monitor that users could zoom in on while scrolling, creating an immersive experience. It was an exciting and unconventional approach that reminded me of the primary principle I established back in 2018: to keep my website simple.

I wanted to go one level beyond and talk about what does all this meant to me, as if the idea sparked something. I knew my about page was a bit out dated. I had not looked at it since 2019. I knew what I needed to do now. UPDATE MY ABOUT PAGE

It became evident that I needed to start afresh and rebuild my about page from the ground level. I began by outlining the key aspects that were most important to me for the about page. I primarily focused on adding a lot about my hobbies and things outside work while making sure I touch base on them and go a bit in detail. The page story:
Working on my portfolio website is a great learning experience for me, I learned a variety of skills from branding, design to development.

This website is still evolving. It excites me every time I look at data and try to figure out things that can be improved. There are a number of places where I know the experience can be improved mainly on analysing the effect of latest changes and where to take this forward.
Till then stay tuned :)

The desk served me well for a long time, but my work outgrew it. Hinge Health, Gojek and Cult.fit each deserved more than a card on a table, and I wanted the site to feel like a journey rather than a page you skim. So I rebuilt the home page as a small universe you fly through.

Ever since my first version in 2018, I wanted my portfolio to reflect not just my work but also who I am. When I sat down to redo it this time, I knew one thing for sure: I didn’t want the first thing people see to be only about healthcare or only about my current job. My career has been a lot more than one place.

Hinge Health, Gojek, Cult.fit, IIT Roorkee and Pibit are all very different, with their own people, their own problems and their own way of doing things. Each one felt like its own little world. So that’s what they became. Every company is a planet, built from scratch in its own brand colours, with a small sign of the work on it: a heartbeat around Hinge Health, a delivery route around Gojek and a running track around Cult.fit. The work I did there orbits it as moons.

I also didn’t want any of it to be just decoration. The bigger the planet, the longer I spent there, and the further apart two planets are, the more years sit between them. Here are three of them at the same scale. Hinge Health is the biggest because I have been there the longest, and Gojek, where I spent about a year and a half, is the smallest. So even without reading a word, the sky tells you the story of my career.

caps: Hinge Health, 2023 – now. A heartbeat runs around it.
Gojek, 2022 – 2023. A delivery route, pickup to drop.

blocks.html: And it doesn’t stop at work. After the planets come my earlier stops, my writing and my life off duty, all in the same sky. In 2023 the story of my about page was “Life is more than work”, and the universe finally let me put all of it in one place.

blocks.cap: Life is more than work: anime, games, books, lifting and the people who matter most, in the same sky as the work.

blocks.text: How I built it, step by step

blocks.html: 1. A small experiment. It started with a chrome shader on my logo, just to see how it would look. That got me looking at the whole site again, starting with what my hero should say. Before the universe, I tried a few other directions.

caps: A chrome shader on my K, where it all started.
Back to a desk, with every prop as its own piece and real shadows.
A studio-light hero, with the logo glitching between materials.

blocks.html: 2. The sky. Next I tried an aurora and kept tuning it until it felt like a real one, light against a dark sky. That’s when it clicked: scrolling should feel like going into space, not down a page.

3. Companies become planets. I made each planet from scratch in that company’s colours, then made them a bit quirky instead of realistic, with a sign of the brand on each. An early Cult.fit planet had a person inside it, but it didn’t match the others, so it went. The quirky side shows best in the cartoon look.

caps: Hinge Health as a physio exercise ball, with a pulse running around its ring.
Cult.fit with a running track for a ring, start line and runner included.

blocks.html: 4. Giving size a meaning. Planet size became the time I spent there and distance became the years in between, like the three planets above. A small readout in the corner, like “2026 · Hinge Health · 1 of 3”, tells you where you are on the way. And for anyone in a hurry, Skip the flight lays the whole journey out on one page.

blocks.cap: Skip the flight: ten years and five teams on one page, newest first.

blocks.html: 5. Filling the rest of the sky. After the main planets I added one view for all my earlier stops, including IIT Roorkee and Pibit, then my writing and life off duty. The about part kept getting longer, so I cut it back. Too much text there felt like too much.

blocks.cap: Where it started: IIT Roorkee, Pibit, my Cult.fit internships and the freelance and contract work in between.

blocks.html: 6. Two looks, side by side. I built a realistic version and a cartoon version in parallel. I couldn’t pick one, so I merged them into a single page.
7. Landing on a moon. Case studies became moon surfaces, and going back zooms you out to the sky. My first version zoomed the whole screen, which felt wrong, so now only the moon you click grows.

8. Launch, then polish. The live version glitched on phones and the scroll felt heavy, so the next few days went into making the flight smooth. A few weeks later I came back to fix the first load, more on that below.

Scrolling moves the camera, not the page. You start at Hello, pass About, then visit each company as a planet in the order I got there: Hinge Health, Gojek and Cult.fit. After that come my earlier stops, my writing, life off duty and finally a way to say hello. A small route map at the bottom always shows where you are, and Skip the flight opens an overview for anyone in a hurry.

I couldn’t decide between a realistic space look and a playful cartoon one, so I kept both. A toggle in the top bar switches between them and the site remembers your choice. Both looks use exactly the same content.

Each planet carries its case studies as moons. Click one and that moon grows from where you clicked until its surface fills the screen, then the case study fades in from it. Back to orbit does the reverse: the moon shrinks to a dot and you are back where you left off. It is all plain CSS transitions, so it stays fast.

The first working version looked right but didn’t feel right. The flight stuttered while scrolling, and on phones it felt heavy. Almost all of it came down to the animation loop doing far more work than it needed to, 60 times a second.

rows: The loop asked the browser for sizes and positions on every frame, which forces it to recalculate the whole layout each time. Now everything is measured once (on load, on resize and when fonts arrive) and the loop only reads the saved numbers.
Elements were looked up again on every frame. Now they are found once at the start and reused.
Each moon asked “am I being hovered?” on every frame. Now it simply listens for the pointer entering and leaving.
Scenes far from the camera were still being updated. Now they are hidden once and skipped until they come close again, and the hero cards only animate near the top.
The year and planet readout at the bottom was rewritten every frame. Now it only updates when the text actually changes.

blocks.html: Smooth scrolling is nice until it feels like the page is dragging behind you. I made the smoothing lighter so it tracks the wheel more closely, and phones now use their own native touch scrolling. Snapping to the next scene only happens on desktop, only once the page has fully stopped, and any wheel movement cancels it. On phones each scene is also a shorter scroll, so you are not swiping forever.
The case study transitions follow the same rule: plain CSS, with no animation loops, blur or filters, so the browser can hand them straight to the graphics card.

A few weeks after launching the universe, I noticed it lagged sometimes. Not every time, which made it even more annoying, and mostly right at the start when the page first loads. That is the worst place it could happen.

Back in 2018 I wrote that the people visiting my portfolio are busy and decide within a few seconds if they want to stay. That is still true. Someone opening my site for the first time doesn’t know about the planets or the moons yet. All they get is those first few seconds, and if those seconds stutter, the whole idea of a journey you fly through falls apart before it even starts. The first load is the first impression, and I wanted to make sure it lands well.

blocks.text: 1. Don’t make it faster, make it smooth

blocks.html: The quick fix would have been to speed up the entrance so there is less time for things to go wrong. I didn’t want that. The slow arrival into space is a big part of the feeling. It was never too slow, it just shouldn’t lag. So I kept the entrance exactly as it was and looked at what was getting in its way.

Most of it came down to the sky. The aurora and the stars take a moment to wake up, and they were waking up right when people started scrolling. A few small decorations were also busy redrawing themselves in the middle of a flight, when nobody could even see them.

blocks.text: 2. The stars have to be there

blocks.html: One option was to show the page first and let the stars come in later. I tried it and the sky only showed up after 4–5 seconds, which felt very slow. I also tried a simple static starfield as a placeholder. It looked awful next to the real sky. Without stars it doesn’t feel like space at all, and then what’s the point of a universe? So the stars had to be there from the very first frame.

blocks.text: 3. A loader, but a tiny one

blocks.html: If the sky needs a moment, I would rather give it that moment than fake it. So I added a short loader. I had a few rules for it: keep it very simple, don’t add anything to the load, and make it feel like it belongs to the universe. It’s a circle with a few stars moving around it, in both the realistic and the cartoon look, so it matches whichever one you picked.
The first version felt a bit plain, so I gave it a little personality from my logo. The K in the middle gives a small nudge, like it is getting ready for take-off.

blocks.cap: The loader in both looks: a ring, a few orbiting stars and my K.

blocks.html: It stays for at least half a second so it never just flashes, and never more than a couple of seconds so nobody is left waiting. If you start scrolling early it gets out of your way, and if you are coming back from a case study you won’t see it again.

The first scroll is smooth now. It went from 8–9 dropped frames to almost none, and the flight to my earlier stops got smoother too. The trade-off is that the first view now comes in about a second later, behind the loader. For me that was an easy call. I would rather someone waits a second and lands in a full, smooth sky than gets there faster and watches it stutter. A first impression only happens once.

It’s not perfect yet. Jumping straight to Hinge Health from the route map can still freeze for a moment before the planet pops in, and the particles react to the mouse a little differently than they used to. Both are next.

From my first site in 2018, to blog cards, a colour-neutral rebrand, a desk and now a universe. Every version taught me something new about storytelling, data and building things myself. This is the final stage of the story, for now, and you are already in it.
